title: Gandalf
description: Fictional character created by J. R. R. Tolkien
wiki_lead:
Gandalf, in longer form Gandalf the Grey and later Gandalf the White, is a protagonist in J. R. R. Tolkien's novels The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. He is a wizard, one of the Istari order, and the leader of the Company of the Ring. Tolkien took the name "Gandalf" from the Old Norse list Dvergatal ("Catalogue of Dwarves") in the Völuspá.
As a wizard and the bearer of one of the Three Rings, Gandalf has great power, but works mostly by encouraging and persuading. He sets out as Gandalf the Grey, possessing great knowledge and travelling continually. Gandalf is focused on the mission to counter the Dark Lord Sauron by destroying the One Ring. He is associated with fire; his ring of power is Narya, the Ring of Fire. As such, he delights in fireworks to entertain the hobbits of the Shire, while in great need he uses fire as a weapon. As one of the Maiar, he is an immortal spirit from Valinor, but his physical body can be killed.
In The Hobbit, Gandalf assists the 13 dwarves and the hobbit Bilbo Baggins with their quest to retake the Lonely Mountain from Smaug the dragon, but leaves them to urge the White Council to expel Sauron from his fortress of Dol Guldur. In the course of the quest, Bilbo finds a magical ring. The expulsion succeeds, but in The Lord of the Rings, Gandalf reveals that Sauron's retreat was only a feint, as he soon reappeared in Mordor. Gandalf further explains that, after years of investigation, he is sure that Bilbo's ring is the One Ring that Sauron needs to dominate the whole of Middle-earth. The Council of Elrond creates the Fellowship of the Ring, with Gandalf as its leader, to defeat Sauron by destroying the Ring. He takes them south through the Misty Mountains, but is killed fighting a Balrog, an evil spirit-being, in the underground realm of Moria. After he dies, he is sent back to Middle-earth to complete his mission as Gandalf the White. He reappears to three of the Fellowship and helps to counter the enemy in Rohan, then in Gondor, and finally at the Black Gate of Mordor, in each case largely by offering guidance. When victory is complete, he crowns Aragorn as King before leaving Middle-earth for ever to return to Valinor.
Tolkien once described Gandalf as an angel incarnate; later, both he and other scholars have likened Gandalf to the Norse god Odin in his "Wanderer" guise. Others have described Gandalf as a guide-figure who assists the protagonists, comparable to the Cumaean Sibyl who assisted Aeneas in Virgil's The Aeneid, or to the figure of Virgil in Dante's Inferno. Scholars have likened his return in white to the transfiguration of Christ; he is further described as a prophet, representing one element of Christ's threefold office of prophet, priest, and king, where the other two roles are taken by Frodo and Aragorn.
The Gandalf character has been featured in radio, television, stage, video game, music, and film adaptations, including Ralph Bakshi's 1978 animated film. His best-known portrayal is by Ian McKellen in Peter Jackson's 2001–2003 The Lord of the Rings film series, where the actor based his acclaimed performance on Tolkien himself. McKellen reprised the role in Jackson's 2012–2014 film series The Hobbit.

grok_lead: Gandalf is a fictional character created by J.R.R. Tolkien, appearing as a wise and enigmatic wizard in the fantasy novels The Hobbit, published in 1937, and The Lord of the Rings, published in three volumes between 1954 and 1955. He is one of the Istari, a small group of Maiarâangelic beingsâwho were sent by the Valar (guardians of the world) to Middle-earth in the Third Age, incarnated in the forms of elderly men to guide the free peoples against the rising threat of the Dark Lord Sauron without dominating them through force. Known initially as Gandalf the Grey for his weathered appearance and grey robes, he later becomes Gandalf the White after a transformative ordeal, symbolizing his elevated authority and renewed purpose in the fight against evil. Appearance and Personality Gandalf is consistently described as an old man of indeterminate but ancient age, with a tall, lean frame, long white hair, a flowing beard, bushy eyebrows, and piercing eyes that convey both warmth and intensity. He wears a tall pointed blue hat, a long grey cloak, a silver scarf, and carries a wooden staff that serves as both a walking aid and a channel for his magic; his weather-beaten face and habit of pipe-smoking add to his folksy, grandfatherly demeanor. Personality-wise, Gandalf embodies wisdom tempered by humor and impatienceâhe is patient and encouraging with the untested, like hobbits, yet stern and commanding when necessary, often delivering cryptic advice or rebukes that spur others to action. His fondness for simple pleasures, such as fireworks, storytelling, and pipe-weed, contrasts with his profound insight into the greater perils facing Middle-earth, earning him respect and affection from diverse races including Elves (who call him Mithrandir, meaning "Grey Pilgrim" or "Grey Wanderer") and Men. Role in The Hobbit In The Hobbit, Gandalf arrives unexpectedly at the home of the hobbit Bilbo Baggins, recruiting him to join a company of thirteen Dwarves led by Thorin Oakenshield on a perilous quest to reclaim their ancestral home, Erebor, from the dragon Smaug. Acting as the group's guide and protector, he uses his knowledge of the wilds and alliances with creatures like the Eagles and Beorn to navigate dangers, while his subtle foresight helps identify Bilbo's latent courage. Though he departs midway to investigate the growing shadow of the Necromancer (later revealed as Sauron) in Dol Guldur, Gandalf's interventionsâsuch as conjuring protective fire or a blinding flash against goblinsâprove crucial to the company's survival. His reputation as a fireworks-maker and adventurer precedes him, making him a beloved figure in the Shire, though his wanderlust and secretive nature often puzzle those around him. Role in The Lord of the Rings and Broader Legendarium Gandalf's significance expands dramatically in The Lord of the Rings, where he uncovers the corrupting nature of the One Ring possessed by Bilbo's heir, Frodo Baggins, and orchestrates the formation of the Fellowship of the Ring to destroy it in the fires of Mount Doom. As the Fellowship's leader, he confronts ancient evils like the Balrog in the Mines of Moria, where he falls in battle but is resurrected by higher powers as Gandalf the White, returning with amplified strength to rally the free peoples of Rohan, Gondor, and beyond against Sauron's forces in the War of the Ring. His strategic counselâsuch as advising ThÃ©oden's restoration or ThÃ©oden's aid to Gondor âturns the tide of war, emphasizing themes of hope, sacrifice, and moral guidance without direct rule. In Tolkien's wider legendarium, detailed in works like The Silmarillion and Unfinished Tales, Gandalf's true identity as the Maia OlÃ³rin emerges: in Valinor, he was a spirit of knowledge and pity under ManwÃ«, the chief Vala, chosen and his role in kindling courage in others. Ultimately, after Sauron's defeat, Gandalf departs Middle-earth for the Undying Lands, his mission fulfilled. Powers and Influence Though limited by the Istari's mandate to use power sparingly, Gandalf wields subtle magic: igniting flames without tinder, creating bursts of light to repel foes, commanding eagles, and glimpsing distant events or futures through wisdom rather than scrying. In combat, his staff breaks like thunder, and as the White, he exudes an aura that scatters shadows. Tolkien drew inspiration for Gandalf from Norse mythology, particularly Odin the wanderer, blending the archetype of the sage mentor with Christian undertones of self-sacrifice and resurrection. This character has profoundly shaped modern fantasy, influencing depictions of wizards as flawed yet indispensable guides in literature, film, and games.
